disease_info: Binge-Eating Disorder (BED) is characterized by recurrent episodes of eating unusually large amounts of food within a discrete time period, accompanied by a sense of loss of control over eating, and followed by marked distress. Unlike bulimia nervosa, individuals with BED do not regularly engage in inappropriate compensatory behaviors such as purging, fasting, or excessive exercise, and weight status can range from normal to obese. Episodes often occur in response to emotional stress, negative mood, or interpersonal difficulties, and the disorder is frequently associated with shame, secrecy, and impaired quality of life. The course can be chronic or fluctuating, with many patients presenting only after weight gain, medical concerns, or functional and emotional consequences become difficult to manage.

narrative.stressor: About fourteen months ago, Fumi increased her night-shift hours as a commercial cleaner after dropping to part-time status in community college, telling herself she would use the flexible schedule to build a design portfolio but instead finding her days and nights increasingly unstructured. Long stretches alone in office buildings, irregular meal breaks, and easy access to vending machines and leftover catered food gradually turned late-night snacking into a habitual way to stay awake and unwind after stressful shifts and creative blocks. As her art projects stalled and she felt further from her dream of becoming a designer, she became more reliant on solitary eating at odd hours to cope with frustration and the guilt of procrastinated coursework and paperwork. She finally sought psychiatric care when her eating patterns began to feel out of control, she noticed significant weight gain affecting her comfort playing basketball and running with the club, and a supervisor’s comment about "raiding the breakroom" left her embarrassed enough to bring it up at a campus counseling center referral.
narrative.chief_complaint: I feel like once I start eating after my night shifts, I can’t stop or control how much I’m eating.

narrative.stressor: George’s difficulties intensified around the time he stepped back from steady event-planning work about a year and a few months ago, after a string of canceled contracts and burnout from constantly being "on" at community festivals. Losing the structure, public recognition, and steady income of his role left him spending more time at home, where cooking large, elaborate meals became both a creative outlet and a way to fill the social void left by fewer events and rec-league games due to nagging knee pain. Over the following year, what started as celebratory feasts for family and church friends increasingly shifted to him preparing big spreads late at night and eating most of the food alone, especially after arguments with his spouse about finances and his overcommitting to unpaid projects. He came to psychiatric attention after his primary care doctor raised concerns about rapid weight gain and rising blood pressure, and George admitted that his eating had gotten "out of hand" since leaving regular work, particularly the times he wolfs down huge amounts of food in one sitting.
narrative.chief_complaint: When I get going, I tear through a ton of food really fast, way faster than I ever used to.

narrative.stressor: About fourteen months ago, Janet’s mother, who had been her closest confidante in gardening, quilting, and church activities, died after a brief illness, leaving Janet with a sudden emptiness in her day-to-day routines. In the months that followed, she continued volunteering and attending farmer’s markets, but she found herself coming home to a quiet house and turning more frequently to her kitchen, baking and cooking in large batches that reminded her of family gatherings. What began as comforting herself with familiar Pennsylvania Dutch recipes gradually evolved into regularly preparing and consuming large quantities of food alone late in the evenings, especially after emotionally draining days at the food bank or when she felt guilty for forgetting appointments and letting small responsibilities slip. She sought psychiatric care after noticing her clothes no longer fit, her hiking stamina had declined, and a friend from her quilting circle gently asked if she was "using food to fill the hole" left by her mother, prompting Janet to recognize how much of her grief was playing out through her eating.
narrative.chief_complaint: I keep eating big amounts of food at night even when I’m not really hungry at all.
